rounds.description: The interview began with them asking me to skip introduction and just give one line description of my projects and my role in them. I had 4 projects mentioned, all related to Data Analysis, ML and LLM, GEN AI. So my resume was highly aligned with the role. I had done an internship, so I also explained about my role in that and spoke about a few of my skills. There were 2 interviewers.

tips.text: So identify your strong area and begin with that.
ensure that you cut out all the noise and stay focused on the day of the interview.
whenever interviewer asks u about a question, try to question him back, to get complete understanding of his question if you did not understand something.

Do not lie about anything, first interview rounds are completely based on your resume. If you dont know about anything that is written it gives a bad impression. Know about every project in detail. Its ok to not know a lot of things, just know whatever you have written.
Also mention those things at the top which you want the interviewer to see, there is no specific order.
3-4 projects are enough, some skills.

Pls do mention about any sports you would have played in your life. My MSCI and IDFC first round interviewers were very interested in my cricket skills and that really helped me. Just add one line but do add.
You dont need to have the best projects, you can have okish projects but need to know everything you did. You can take them from github, but again, know everything.
If you can deploy them somewhere, that can be good as you can show it live to interviewer. But that is absolutely not necessary.

If you are asked something you dont know about, there are 2 ways,either you have absolutely now idea about it- just say sir i am not aware about it. Or you can relate it to some other topic. In that case mention that i dont know exactly, but i feel this is similar to the other thing i have worked on.
First round is just resume based, no need to worry much.
Also just to impress the interviewer dont speak fancy words which you are not aware of or have good knowledge about.

DSA is necessary, but 500-700 problems are not, you can crack the best of companies even with less problems solved. But the more you solve, the more confidence you will have of solving unseen problems in oa or interview.
Confidence is really important in dsa as in the pressure if you cant think of the right approach, it can get difficult.
Codeforces, CP is absolutely not needed for any company other than PHONE PE. I still havent solved any problem on codeforces.
If you like solving thats great but please ensure you are working on other aspects also.
Also do ensure that you can take input in your language, as leetcode does not prepare us for that.
Leetcode contests solving can be helpful, to get practice but dont panic if you can solve only 1 or two problems or even if you cant solve any problem in a contest.
You can directly skip HARD problems on LC.
Follow strivers A2Z Sheet.
Even if you have not solved many problems, in june try to read through all easy-medium problems in strivers sheet. Having an idea can help you atleast come up with an approach in interviews.
Java oops are extremely important, dbms comes next, along with sql, os is slightly important, while ccn mostly wont be asked, although its good to know basics.
Please participate in hacks. If you dont have the confidence, or no one is taking you in their team, find 3 others like you and participate.

Because A- it gives you some impactful projects and B- if you sincerely give your best for 24 hours, for 4-5 hacks you will eventually win one for sure. It is helpful in interviews as it validates your skills for the interviewer.
Also winning hacks dont require extraordinary skills these days. Just you need to be able to use open source tools well and present well.
Please participate in company hackathons, if you win or even reach finale , they will select you for placement.
Although if you are not able to win, that is not the end of the road, its not at all necessary.

If you have certain preferences its ok to let go of some roles. But please be realistic, if you have confidence in your preparation, only then leave companies. Because it may happen that good companies might go away.
Also please dont be too dependent on one role/company.
At the same time it is important to have a few target companies and give it your all for it.
Overall if you have prepared well, You will do well eventually.
Rejections can be tough, but eventually it will help you get something better.

rounds.name: Technical Round-1
rounds.description: The round began with the interviewer asking me to introduce myself.. I introduced myself, told him about my internship and my contribution to it. Then I talked about my projects, giving him some overview about them, to which he would ask some questions in between regarding them. Then he began asking some basic questions, such as defining data structures like Hashmap, Stack, Queue, LinkedList, etc. This was pretty easy, so I even explained some extra info for each, such as what is collision in hashmap, struct of LinkedList,etc and gave examples for each. I solved both of them very quickly, and the interviewer only needed the logic, no code or pseudocode. Then he asked me briefly about my experience with Flask, React, etc (they were mentioned in the JD), but didn't ask any questions about them. He then asked me if I knew Python, to which I replied that it was my primary language. Then he proceeded with asking multiple questions on Python. I was able to answer all questions except the syntax of the decorator wrapper function. I asked him a question about the role and his experience at the end. The interview lasted for around 35 minutes.

rounds.description: The interviewer looked through my resume and asked me a question on what Apache Kafka is and how it works (it was mentioned on my resume). Then he gave me two tables, and asked me to first tell him what I can infer from it, and then write the SQL query for it. I had messed up a bit initially, to which the interviewer gave me a hint, after which I was able to solve the query. The query included Sub Query, Aggregation, Grouping and Join concepts. After this he began asking me questions on core DBMS. I was able to answer all the questions asked to me, and I tried to always give some extra info related to the solution. The interviewer seemed content with all my answers. After this he was about to ask me a DSA question, but asked to just explain Collision in hashmaps, that's it. At the end I asked him how the transition from college to corporate is, and what was his experience. The interview lasted for around 25-30 minutes.

rounds.name: HR Round
rounds.description: The interview began with the interviewer asking me a brief intro about myself, what I’ve done and what are my skills, and my experience as the Head of Marketing at Oculus. He then asked me about my understanding of the JD. I replied according to what I had researched about it. Then he asked me for the top 3 qualities about myself, and a little about my internship. He then asked me what drives me to do more. Looking at my CGPA, he asked me if I was in the top 30% of my class, and why I was not higher. Then he asked me a tricky question, which was “When should one do MBA” (he wanted to check if i had any plans for it). I turned it around by stating that the correct question should be “Why MBA”, and started building around it. He proceeded to ask me questions about my family background and where I live. He also mentioned that my travel from Colaba to Powai won’t be so joyous, to which I said I'm accustomed to it, and might consider shifting. He asked me to rate myself in coding, what would be my actions if someone is better at it, at work, and what ratio would I draw between tech and finance market during my work. Lastly, I made comments on how I'm a good fit for the role, as the role serves both verticals of Tech and Finance, and I have the appropriate technical, communication skills and the business acumen required.

rounds.description: It began with the interviewer asking me to introduce myself and talk a bit about my internship and projects, and how I did them. She then said she’ll be asking me questions on Python, to which I thought it would be like the last round, but it wasn't the case. She began by asking me what's the difference between loc and iloc. I thought she meant about the ‘Lock’ in threading in python, to which i explained everything. She then told me she means loc and iloc in Pandas. At the end, I made a statement that although the interview started on the wrong note, as I wasn't able to give the syntax for Pandas, I’m a quick learner and can adapt well to new technologies, instances of which I have proved earlier. To this she said it's alright. The interview lasted for around 45 minutes.

She told me that there’s a lot of electronic data coming in continuously, and we only have limited memory resources. So how would I process the data? I told her that I would use Pagination to split the incoming data into chunks, then use multithreading to parallelly process the data, with each thread responsible for some chunk of data, and finally use the garbage collector to discard threads not in use. Then she asked me about my hobbies and if I had any questions. By the end the interview almost became a bit casual, we were almost just conversing at that point. tips.text: Try to keep your CG above 8

It's very very important to not lose hope or give up. Right till the start of my 3rd year, I was planning to do Non Tech and not even sit for tech companies. But my internship changed my perspective. I started DSA, more dev, and things started falling into place. So even if you haven't started yet, it’s never too late. Just work hard and give it your all.
Luck is a major major factor in placements. Do not underestimate it, but also do not let it affect you as well.
Resume building is very crucial. Know the format well, ONLY INCLUDE WHAT YOU ARE CONFIDENT ABOUT, learn the concepts if you have lied on your resume.
Pick a programming language to master. I chose Python. Companies prefer Java a lot, almost all of them. So maybe go for that or C++, and practice Python every now and then.
Giving contests on Leetcode or Codeforces (again, Competitive Programming can help a lot, it’s not required though). This will help you learn to code under time constraints.

Build your communication skills, very important for interviews. Maybe help each other by taking each other’s interviews. I had been good at it, so I didn't prepare much. But one can rehearse, get some tips from youtube and participate in competitions for it.

It is very important to know how to answer your interviewers be it Tech or HR. Always greet when you enter, wait for their offer to take a seat, greet when leaving. These minor things leave an impact.

Know how to build stories around your answers from past experiences, or maybe even lie a little, elaborate on your answers, give some extra information to what you’re asked to show how you stand out. These things specifically help in HR rounds a lot.

Prepare a good introduction about yourself. It should include the following points: First greet and thank for the opportunity Name, degree, college and year. Where you’ve been born and brought up (cover this in like 2 short sentences max) A brief about your skills (like good fundamentals in Full Stack Development or Machine Learning, built scalable projects) Mention your internship experience if you have any in 2-3 lines, what you did there and how it was for you Give an overview of 1 or 2 of your projects, what they are and what they solve. Unless asked for, don't explain more projects. Then cover any extracurricular activities apart from Tech, like I was the Head of Marketing for Oculus. Your experience in it and what you did. Move on to any achievements, competitions, hobbies (all of this in one line) And lastly, but most importantly, briefly explain why you are a good fit for the role by matching with JD and covering your skills. Any introduction anywhere between 30 seconds to 1.5 minutes is good enough.
DSA is not only going to get you better at Data Structures and Algorithms, but also build your logical thinking and fluency with the language you code in.
Prepare for OOPS, preferably in Java, and the language you are confident about.
Prepare for DBMS and SQL from Love Babbar’s videos.
Prepare for Puzzles and Guestimmates as well.
You can prepare for System Design as well, which I have done. Even if it’s not asked directly, it improves your understanding of concepts very well. Although you can easily skip this.
GFG is great for questions on Core Concepts (OS, CCN, Language specific)
Prepare Aptitude questions from IndiaBix
Have at least 3 projects ready. They shouldn’t be too simple, having some impact is always appreciated. Projects on Development or Machine Learning are the most common.
Actively participate in Hackathons, maybe even Case Study Competitions (it will give you more confidence)

tips.text: Prepare a solid Introduction covering everything in your resume and focusing on stuff you are confident at.

Whenever given a question, walk through the entire solution from start to finish with the interviewer. They are more interested in how you are approaching the problem. If you don't know something, ask for a hint but don't go silent.
Practice DSA so that even if a simple question is asked you are able to confidently answer it.
Prepare all your Projects in your resume thoroughly. From tech stack to why did you use that tech stack. Whatever you use in your projects, lets say MERN, read top interview questions for it.
Dont try to force something that u dont know because if they ask questions and you are not able to answer it leaves a bad impression.
Practice SQL top 50 on leetcode.
The key point for HR is to answer everything honestly.
Don't prepare a lot before this round.
Read a bit about the company and JD.
Write only the stuff in your resume that you are able to answer.
Read about the company and the JD before sitting for the interviews.
Keep smiling and appear confident

Try to polish your communication skills as this is how the interviewer judges you. If you are not able to communicate your answer to the interviewer then it doesn’t matter if your answer was perfect. Mock interviews are of great help in this aspect.
Ask questions in the end related to their role in the company or something else you are curious about
DSA, SQL, DBMS, OOPS are some of the most important concepts
Try to learn JAVA as well, but if you don't know, it's nothing to worry about. The interviewers want to check if you are ready to learn and quick to learn.

It is not important to have very unique and different project. A decent enough project is fine but make sure you know in and out about the project(Why did you use the tech stack? Why not something else?).
Read top interview questions of your tech stack as well

tips.text: check in advance if a calculator is allowed.
If calculators aren’t allowed, I suggest using the round-off method to reach the closest answer faster.
Start with the Verbal section — passages and sentence-based questions were straightforward. Quants was easy too, but DI can eat up time if you don’t plan ahead.
If Nomura is visiting other colleges a day or two before, try to connect with students from those campuses — the topics and question patterns are often similar.
While introducing yourself, explain a basic overview of your best-known project — this helps you lead the interview in a direction you’re comfortable with.
Always think aloud — even if the interviewer pretends to be busy, they are paying attention to how you approach a problem, not just the final solution.
They don’t expect perfect answers they value your approach, logic and thought process more. Write down whatever valid, strong ideas you have.
In any round, explain your thoughts well , clarity and confidence matters!
Always use words you’re confident about, and never fake your resume ,they read every single line carefully.
Be confident about whatever you say — but also make sure it’s logically sound.
Don’t bluff — honesty stands out more than pretending to know everything.
They test how you think, not just how much you know.
Be honest, don’t fake your resume , they do read every line and grill you on it. Only mention skills and projects you truly know.

If you haven’t started with DSA yet, don’t panic! Just do NeetCode 75, focus on understanding how to approach and solve problems, not just memorizing solutions. In real interviews, even a brute force solution works if you explain your thought process well. Knowing an optimized version is always better but the approach is what they test first.
For aptitude, IndiaBix is gold. Don’t stop at the first few pages of any topic — the later questions are often more relevant and closer to real test patterns.
Keep a smiling face and maintain a pleasant vibe , a positive attitude goes a long way, even when you don’t know an answer.
Be open to discussions. If you’re wrong or stuck, don’t bluff , justify your thoughts, explain your logic. They care about how you think, not just about “perfect” answers.
Control what you can , but remember, LUCK PLAYS A BIG ROLE TOO! Focus on your preparation, stay confident, and trust the process.

rounds.description: This round started at around 10 am. I was asked to introduce myself. It happened before the written OA test. Most of the early questions were based on my resume. I had mentioned a Spring Boot project and told him that Java is my primary programming language. So the next 80% of our discussion revolved around Spring Framework, Java and OOPS. He asked me about inheritance and polymorphism and gave me different scenarios. Also I was asked about binary search tree, quick sort algo and time complexity in general. Next I was given a simple SQL query and asked some HR type questions. Then we just talked casually about the entire placement process and asked me about my experience throughout the journey. At this point we were having just a normal conversation about stuff and he asked if I had any questions for him to which I asked a couple and the interview ended. This was a pretty chill experience for me since all the topics we discussed we my favs.

rounds.name: Technical Interview - 2
rounds.description: This round started at around 2:30 pm post lunch. There were 2 interviewers in each panel for this round. He asked me to give my introduction but nothing from my resume lol. We started by discussing Spring Framework (yet again yess) and how it differs from MERN, its benefits and widespread use cases. We talked about JUnit testing and how unit testing works further delving into different types of testing methodologies. They went through my resume and asked me detailed questions about the technical skills that I had mentioned in the resume. I was asked questions about MERN stack and databases used in my projects. We had a discussion about JWT and how it works. I was also asked about Hadoop and how it works (I had mentioned hadoop on my resume). We also talked about how Spring Security works and how it is different from some other ways to secure web applications. We discussed about Stripe (used in a project) payment gateway which is similar to razorpay and how it works. This was a relatively shorter round than the first one (1st was 75 minutes long ) which lasted around 40 minutes.

tips.text: It is recommended to have your webcam on and ask questions during the pre-placement talk.
I’d recommend solving the verbal and analytical questions first and then moving on to the quants as this section is time consuming.
Some questions are purely in the test to waste your time. Try and identify these types of questions and keep them for the end.
Have 4-5 good projects covering important domains and use them appropriately for the JD you’re applying for.
Interviewers often ask 2-3 niche questions to try and shake your confidence. In such times, try and steer the discussion to the nearest relatable topic/case you can think of instead of saying idk.
For vague questions or scenarios be upfront and ask them the details before assuming especially for puzzles and dsa questions.
Solving even about 150 varied and good quality problems are enough.
For SQL, leetcode-sql-50 will suffice (I personally did the first 30 only lol).
Indiabix and Interviewbit are helpful.
Make sure every single thing mentioned on your resume is relevant and you have sufficient knowledge about the topics and projects mentioned.
Questions related to tech stack used, not used, why, how, are litmus tests for interviewers to test your technical knowledge and skills so be prepared for them.
The first few interviews might feel a bit overwhelming, but once you get the hang of it things get pretty easy. Keep a smile and just be yourself.
Try and compose yourself and use the experience from negative results to iteratively work on weaknesses and better yourself.
have trust in your abilities and Keep giving your best cuz you only need luck to be on your side just once.
